steps.text: **Step 1: Define real and virtual images**

cards.problem: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror perpendicular to its surface. What is the angle of reflection?

steps.text: **Step 1: Define normal and angle of incidence**
The normal is an imaginary line perpendicular to the mirror surface.
If a ray strikes the mirror perpendicularly, it is aligned with the normal.
Therefore, the angle between the incident ray and the normal is:
**Step 2: Apply the law of reflection**
$$r = i = 0^\circ$$
**Step 3: Final Result**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A spherical mirror has a radius of curvature of $$R = 30.0\text{ cm}$$. What is the focal length ($$f$$) of this mirror if it is concave?
cards.why:
**Step 1: State the relationship between radius and focal length**  
$$f = \frac{R}{2}$$

**Step 2: Apply sign conventions**  
For a concave (converging) mirror, the focal length is positive ($$f > 0$$):
$$f = +\frac{30.0\text{ cm}}{2} = 15.0\text{ cm}$$

**Step 3: Final Result**  
The focal length of the concave mirror is **$$15.0\text{ cm}$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What are the constant characteristics of an image formed by a convex (diverging) mirror for any real object?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze convex mirror optics**  
For a convex mirror, the focal length is negative ($$f < 0$$). Tracing incident parallel rays shows they diverge and their virtual extensions meet behind the mirror.

**Step 2: Determine image properties**  
The image is always located behind the mirror (virtual), oriented upright (erect), and smaller than the object (diminished).

**Step 3: Final Result**  
The characteristics are **Virtual, erect, and diminished**.

cards.title: 5.1 Nature, Sources, and Transmission of Light
body: **Light** is a form of electromagnetic radiation that can be detected by the human eye, propagating in straight lines called rays and carrying energy through empty space or material media.

cards.title: 5.1 Nature, Sources, and Transmission of Light — Deep Dive (1/2)
body: Geometrical optics is the branch of physics that studies the propagation of light under the approximation that light behaves as a stream of particles moving along straight lines, called rays. In a homogeneous, isotropic medium, light rays travel in strictly straight lines—a fundamental principle known as the **rectilinear propagation of light**. This straight-line behavior explains many everyday optical phenomena, such as the formation of sharp shadows when an opaque object blocks a light source, and the operation of a **pinhole camera**, which produces a real, inverted image on a screen without using lenses.

Objects in our universe are classified based on their ability to emit light. **Luminous objects** generate and emit their own light through internal energy transformations (such as chemical, thermal, or nuclear processes). Examples include the Sun, stars, burning candles, and electric light bulbs. **Non-luminous (or illuminated) objects** do not produce their own light; instead, they become visible only when they reflect light from a luminous source into our eyes. Examples include the Moon, planets, books, walls, and human beings.

When light encounters a boundary with a material, its transmission behavior depends on the atomic structure of the medium. **Transparent materials** (such as clear glass, water, and air) allow almost all incident light to pass through them with negligible scattering, allowing objects behind them to be seen clearly. **Translucent materials** (such as frosted glass, oiled paper, and thin tissue) allow some light to pass through but scatter the rays in random directions, preventing clear images from forming. **Opaque materials** (such as wood, iron, and stone) do not permit any light to pass through; they either reflect or absorb the incident electromagnetic energy.

cards.title: 5.1 Nature, Sources, and Transmission of Light — Deep Dive (2/2)
body: Why it matters: The rectilinear propagation of light allows us to model complex optical systems using simple geometry. This forms the basis for designing spectacles, cameras, telescopes, and solar eclipses prediction. It also explains how light travels through the vast vacuum of space from distant stars to reach our planet, proving that light does not require a material medium to propagate.

cards.title: 5.1 Nature, Sources, and Transmission of Light — Comparison of Optical Materials
body: Material Class — Light Transmission — Ray Behavior — Practical Examples | Transparent — Highly efficient ($$\approx 90\%+$$) — Straight-line propagation without scattering — Optical glass, pure water, clean air | Translucent — Partial transmission — Scattered and diffused in random directions — Frosted glass, tracing paper, fog | Opaque — Zero transmission — Absorbed or reflected at the surface — Wood, steel, concrete, human skin

> **💡 Did You Know?**: The pinhole camera (or *camera obscura*) was known to ancient philosophers like Aristotle and Mozi. During a partial solar eclipse, the small gaps between the leaves of a tree act as natural pinholes, projecting hundreds of tiny, crescent-shaped images of the eclipsed Sun onto the ground below!

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: In pinhole camera calculations, remember that the ratio of image size to object size is equal to the ratio of image distance to object distance: $$\frac{h_i}{h_o} = \frac{d_i}{d_o}$$. Use this simple geometry to solve any camera scale problem.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A light ray strikes a plane mirror. If the angle between the incident ray and the mirror's flat surface is $$40^\circ$$, what is the angle of incidence?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand the geometric definitions**  
The normal is perpendicular ($$90^\circ$$) to the mirror surface. The angle between the incident ray and the surface is given as $$40^\circ$$.

**Step 2: Calculate the angle of incidence ($$i$$)**  
The angle of incidence is measured from the normal:
$$i = 90^\circ - 40^\circ = 50^\circ$$

**Step 3: Final Result**  
The angle of incidence is **$$50^\circ$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following optical phenomena is a direct consequence of the rectilinear propagation of light?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define rectilinear propagation of light**  
Rectilinear propagation means that light travels in strictly straight lines within a homogeneous medium.

**Step 2: Analyze shadow formation**  
When an opaque object is placed in front of a light source, the straight-line rays cannot curve around the object. Consequently, the region directly behind the object remains unlit, creating a sharp shadow.

**Step 3: Final Result**  
Therefore, the **Formation of shadows** is a direct consequence.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If the angle of incidence of a light ray striking a flat mirror is increased, what happens to the angle of reflection?

options.B: It increases by the same amount.

cards.why:
**Step 1: State the second law of reflection**  
$$r = i$$
This means the angle of reflection ($$r$$) must always equal the angle of incidence ($$i$$).

**Step 2: Analyze changes**  
If $$i$$ increases, $$r$$ must increase by the exact same amount to maintain the equality.

**Step 3: Final Result**  
The angle of reflection **increases by the same amount**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If an object is placed at the principal focus ($$F$$) of a concave mirror, where is the image formed?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Apply the mirror equation**  
$$\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{d_o} + \frac{1}{d_i}$$
Since the object is at the focus, $$d_o = f$$:
$$\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{f} + \frac{1}{d_i} \implies \frac{1}{d_i} = 0 \implies d_i = \infty$$

**Step 2: Analyze ray behavior**  
Light rays originating from the focus reflect parallel to the principal axis. Parallel lines only meet at infinity.

**Step 3: Final Result**  
The image is formed **at infinity**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What happens to the image of your face in a plane mirror as you step further away from the mirror?

options.C: The image remains the same size and moves further behind the mirror.
options.D: The image becomes real and inverted.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Apply plane mirror laws**  
- The size of the image in a plane mirror is always equal to the object size ($$h_i = h_o$$), which does not depend on distance.
- The image distance is equal to the object distance ($$d_i = d_o$$).

**Step 2: Determine behavior on moving away**  
As you step back (increasing $$d_o$$), the image moves back behind the mirror (increasing $$d_i$$) but remains the same size ($$h_i = h_o$$).

**Step 3: Final Result**  
The image **remains the same size and moves further behind the mirror**.

cards.title: 5.2 Reflection of Light and Plane Mirrors
body: **Reflection of Light** is the physical bouncing back of light rays when they strike the boundary of an opaque medium or a reflective interface.

cards.title: 5.2 Reflection of Light and Plane Mirrors — Deep Dive (1/2)
body: When a ray of light strikes a reflective interface, its behavior is described by a set of geometric parameters. The incoming ray is the **incident ray**, the point where it strikes the surface is the **point of incidence**, and the line perpendicular to the surface at this point is the **normal**. The ray that bounces off the surface is the **reflected ray**. The **Angle of Incidence** ($$i$$) is the angle between the incident ray and the normal, while the **Angle of Reflection** ($$r$$) is the angle between the reflected ray and the normal.

These rays obey the **Laws of Reflection**, which state: 1. The incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same physical plane (called the *plane of incidence*). 2. The angle of incidence is always strictly equal to the angle of reflection ($$i = r$$).

Reflection is classified into two types depending on the surface topography. **Regular (or specular) reflection** occurs when parallel light rays strike a highly polished, perfectly smooth surface (such as a plane mirror or a calm pool of water). In this case, the reflected rays remain parallel, producing a sharp, clear image. **Irregular (or diffuse) reflection** occurs when parallel light rays strike a rough or unpolished surface (such as paper, wood, or a wall). Because the surface has microscopic irregularities, the normal at each point points in a different direction, causing the parallel rays to reflect in random directions. This prevents the formation of an image but allows the surface to be seen from any angle.

Images formed by reflecting surfaces are categorized as either real or virtual. A **real image** is formed when the reflected light rays actually intersect at a physical point in space. Real images are always inverted (upside down) and can be projected onto a physical screen. A **virtual image** is formed when the reflected light rays do not actually intersect but *appear* to diverge from a point behind the mirror. Virtual images are always erect (upright) and cannot be projected onto a screen.

cards.title: 5.2 Reflection of Light and Plane Mirrors — Deep Dive (2/2)
body: A **plane mirror** is a flat, highly polished reflecting surface. The images formed by a plane mirror have five distinct geometric properties: 1. The image is virtual (located behind the mirror where light rays do not actually pass). 2. The image is erect (upright). 3. The image is of the exact same size as the object ($$h_i = h_o$$). 4. The image distance behind the mirror is equal to the object distance in front of the mirror ($$d_i = d_o$$). 5. The image exhibits **lateral inversion**, meaning it is reversed left-to-right (sideways).

cards.title: 5.2 Reflection of Light and Plane Mirrors — Specular vs. Diffuse Reflection
body: Parameter — Specular (Regular) Reflection — Diffuse (Irregular) Reflection | Surface Texture — Highly polished and smooth — Microscopically rough or uneven | Reflected Ray Paths — Parallel rays remain parallel — Parallel rays reflect in random directions | Image Formation — Produces clear, sharp images — Does not produce an image | Laws of Reflection — Obeyed at every point — Obeyed at every point (but local normals differ)

> **💡 Did You Know?**: The lateral inversion of plane mirrors is the reason why the word "AMBULANCE" is printed backward on the front of emergency vehicles. When a driver looks in their rear-view mirror, the lateral inversion of the mirror reverses the text back to its correct orientation, allowing them to read it instantly and yield the way!

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: When calculating reflection angles, always measure from the *normal* line, not from the mirror's surface. If a question states that a ray strikes a mirror at an angle of $$30^\circ$$ to the *surface*, the angle of incidence is $$90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ$$.

cards.title: 5.4 The Mirror Equation, Magnification, and Sign Conventions
body: The **Mirror Equation** is an analytical formula relating the object distance ($$d_o$$), image distance ($$d_i$$), and focal length ($$f$$) of a spherical mirror: $$\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{d_o} + \frac{1}{d_i}$$.

cards.title: 5.3 Spherical Mirrors and Ray Diagrams
body: **Spherical Mirrors** are reflecting surfaces that form a segment of a hollow sphere, classified into concave (converging) and convex (diverging) mirrors depending on which side is reflective.

cards.title: 5.3 Spherical Mirrors and Ray Diagrams — Deep Dive (1/2)
body: Spherical mirrors are widely used in optical systems where light must be converged or diverged. To analyze these mirrors, we must first define several key geometric parameters: • **Pole ($$P$$)**: The geometric center of the spherical mirror surface. • **Center of Curvature ($$C$$)**: The center of the hollow glass sphere of which the mirror forms a segment. • **Radius of Curvature ($$R$$)**: The radius of the hollow sphere ($$PC = R$$). • **Principal Axis**: The straight line passing through both the pole ($$P$$) and the center of curvature ($$C$$). • **Principal Focus ($$F$$)**: The point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis either converge after reflection (for concave mirrors) or appear to diverge from after reflection (for convex mirrors). • **Focal Length ($$f$$)**: The distance from the pole to the principal focus ($$PF = f$$).

For a spherical mirror with a small aperture, the focal length is exactly half of its radius of curvature: $$f = \frac{R}{2} \implies R = 2f$$ This means the principal focus ($$F$$) lies midway between the pole ($$P$$) and the center of curvature ($$C$$).

A **Concave Mirror** has its reflecting surface curved inward (like the inside of a spoon). It is also called a **converging mirror** because it brings parallel incident rays to a real focus in front of the mirror. A **Convex Mirror** has its reflecting surface curved outward (like the back of a spoon). It is also called a **diverging mirror** because it spreads parallel incident rays outward, making them appear to originate from a virtual focus behind the mirror.

To locate and characterize the image formed by a spherical mirror graphically, we construct **ray diagrams** using three principal rays originating from a point on the object: 1. **The Parallel Ray**: An incident ray parallel to the principal axis reflects through the principal focus $$F$$ (for a concave mirror) or appears to diverge from the virtual focus $$F$$ (for a convex mirror). 2. **The Focal Ray**: An incident ray passing through the focus $$F$$ (for a concave mirror) or directed toward the virtual focus $$F$$ (for a convex mirror) reflects parallel to the principal axis.

cards.title: 5.3 Spherical Mirrors and Ray Diagrams — Deep Dive (2/2)
body: **The Center of Curvature Ray**: An incident ray passing through the center of curvature $$C$$ (for a concave mirror) or directed toward the center of curvature $$C$$ (for a convex mirror) strikes the mirror normally and reflects back along its original path. The intersection of any two of these reflected rays determines the position, size, and orientation of the image.

cards.title: 5.3 Spherical Mirrors and Ray Diagrams — Concave vs. Convex Mirrors
body: Feature — Concave (Converging) Mirror — Convex (Diverging) Mirror | Reflecting Surface — Curved inward (inner segment) — Curved outward (outer segment) | Focal Length ($$f$$) — Positive ($$f > 0$$) — Negative ($$f < 0$$) | Image Types Produced — Real and inverted, or Virtual and erect — Strictly Virtual and erect | Image Size — Can be magnified, diminished, or same size — Strictly diminished (smaller than object) | Common Applications — Shaving mirrors, solar cookers, headlights — Passenger-side car mirrors, security mirrors

> **💡 Did You Know?**: Convex mirrors are used in convenience stores and parking garages as security mirrors because they provide a much wider angle of view (field of view) than flat plane mirrors, allowing one to see around blind corners!

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: When drawing ray diagrams, always remember that real rays are drawn with solid lines and arrows, while virtual rays (the extensions behind the mirror surface) are drawn with dashed lines to show that light does not actually pass through that region.

cards.title: 5.4 The Mirror Equation, Magnification, and Sign Conventions — Deep Dive
body: While ray diagrams are useful for visualizing how images are formed, we can calculate the exact position, size, and orientation of an image more quickly and accurately using analytical methods. The mathematical relationship between the object distance ($$d_o$$), image distance ($$d_i$$), and the focal length ($$f$$) of a spherical mirror is given by the **mirror equation**: $$\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{d_o} + \frac{1}{d_i}$$ This equation can be derived geometrically from the triangles formed in a ray diagram under the paraxial approximation (which assumes that the mirror aperture is small and that the rays are close to the principal axis).

To find the relative size of the image compared to the object, we calculate the **linear magnification** ($$m$$). Magnification is defined as the ratio of the height of the image ($$h_i$$) to the height of the object ($$h_o$$): $$m = \frac{h_i}{h_o}$$ Using similar triangles, we can also express magnification in terms of the image and object distances: $$m = -\frac{d_i}{d_o}$$ The negative sign in this equation is a mathematical convention used to indicate the orientation of the image. If the magnification $$m$$ is positive, the image is upright (erect); if $$m$$ is negative, the image is upside down (inverted).

To ensure that the mirror equation and magnification formula yield mathematically consistent results for both concave and convex mirrors, we must follow a strict set of **sign conventions**: 1. **Object Distance ($$d_o$$)**: Positive ($$d_o > 0$$) if the object is in front of the mirror (real object); negative ($$d_o < 0$$) if the object is behind the mirror (virtual object). 2. **Image Distance ($$d_i$$)**: Positive ($$d_i > 0$$) if the image is in front of the mirror (real image); negative ($$d_i < 0$$) if the image is behind the mirror (virtual image). 3. **Focal Length ($$f$$) and Radius ($$R$$)**: Positive ($$f > 0$$) for a concave (converging) mirror; negative ($$f < 0$$) for a convex (diverging) mirror.
**Heights ($$h_o$$ and $$h_i$$)**: Object height $$h_o$$ is always positive. Image height $$h_i$$ is positive if the image is upright (erect) and negative if the image is upside down (inverted).

cards.title: 5.4 The Mirror Equation, Magnification, and Sign Conventions — Summary of Mirror Sign Conventions
body: Optical Parameter — Positive Sign ($$+$$) — Negative Sign ($$-$$) | Object Distance ($$d_o$$) — Real object (in front of mirror) — Virtual object (behind mirror) | Image Distance ($$d_i$$) — Real image (in front of mirror) — Virtual image (behind mirror) | Focal Length ($$f$$) — Concave mirror (converging) — Convex mirror (diverging) | Magnification ($$m$$) — Upright / Erect image (virtual) — Inverted / Upside down image (real)

> **💡 Did You Know?**: Dentists use a small concave mirror to inspect your teeth. When the mirror is positioned very close to a tooth (placing the tooth within the mirror's focal length, $$d_o < f$$), it produces a magnified, upright virtual image behind the mirror, allowing the dentist to spot tiny cavities easily!

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: When solving for image distance ($$d_i$$), you can rearrange the mirror equation to avoid fraction mistakes: $$d_i = \frac{d_o f}{d_o - f}$$. Always keep the signs of $$f$$ and $$d_o$$ in mind when substituting values into this formula!

tips.text: Those objects which produce their own light are called luminous and those which do not produce light are called non-luminous.
Light from a source propagates in all directions.
The propagation of light is represented in terms of a group of rays called a beam of light.
A beam of light can be parallel, diverging or converging.
Different materials allow light to pass through them to varying degrees.
Depending on their power of transmission of light substances are divided into transparent, translucent and opaque materials.
Transparent substances transmit most of the light, translucent materials allow only a smaller part of the light to pass through them, and opaque materials don’t transmit the light at all.
In a uniform medium light travels in a straight line.
The straight line motion of light is called rectilinear propagation of light.
The formation of such an image can only be explained by the fact that light travels along a straight line.
